metadata.title: Claude, Supplier Selection.
metadata.subtitle: The Score Behind the Pick

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. First guess about how Claude picks a supplier: whoever's cheapest. Wrong. It runs a weighted formula. Let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. A Claude skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts — that's the whole trick. This one's called supplier-selection. Open it: one file, SKILL.md. Plain English, no hidden logic. Everything driving the pick sits in text you can read.
The reasonable-sounding read: Claude sorts by price, low quote wins. It optimizes for one thing — cost — and ignores everything else. Simple. Defensible. And wrong.

Open SKILL.md — price is one input, not the answer. The score weighs three things: price fifty percent, lead time thirty, reliability twenty. That ratio is the design choice: cost dominates, but speed and dependability each earn a real vote.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — the weighted score, three factors

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — THE SCORE
production_viz.caption: the weighted score — not price alone

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening inside. Price and lead time get normalized onto a common zero-to-one scale — otherwise you're adding dollars to days, which means nothing. Multiply each factor by its weight, sum them, take the highest. Ties break on price, then lead time, then name. Every step deterministic.

Determinism is the point of a formula — same quotes in, same score out, every time. But here's the trade-off the design accepts: SKILL.md also carries override notes, written in plain English, that never touch the catalog data. When one applies, it beats the top score. The formula gets repeatability; the notes get the last word.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same weights, an override can flip it

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS
production_viz.caption: same weights every time; a written override can still beat the score

beats.narration_text: A Claude skill's pick isn't the cheapest supplier. It's the highest score from a weighted formula — and a note the formula never sees can still beat it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — it walks you through building a weighted-score picker from scratch on any decision worth thinking through. Then go deeper: what's the smallest change to your weights that flips the top pick — and does that fragility mean the weights are wrong, or that two candidates are just genuinely close?

llm_exercise.prompt: Help me design a weighted-score picker for a decision — say, choosing a supplier, a vendor, or a candidate. Walk me through: (1) which factors to include and why, (2) how to normalize inputs that live in different units (dollars, days, percentages) onto a common zero-to-one scale, (3) how to set weights so the ratio matches what I actually care about, and (4) where to leave room for an override note — a fact the formula never sees — that can beat the top score. Show it working on three candidates and three factors, with the math visible at every step.
